Threat.value: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
I feel on guard even inside my own home
I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me

Memory.value: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish
I find myself pushing the memory away before I can fully recall it
Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind.

vignette:
Linh Nguyen was seventy-six, a mechanic who had run her own small garage for forty years, and she had never been afraid of much until the stalking began. It started with a customer—a man whose truck she had repaired twice—who began waiting outside the garage at closing time, standing in the dirt patch beside the bay door where the smell of rain-soaked earth clung to his boots. At first she assumed he was just early for an appointment, but he followed her home, parked down the street, and eventually began leaving notes under the windshield of her old sedan. The police were called, a restraining order was filed, and he disappeared after a few months, but the damage was already done. Now, two years later, Linh could not explain what had happened without losing the thread of her own story—she would start describing the dirt and his shadow, then the sentences would tangle, and she would give up. The memory existed instead as a series of perfect photographs in her mind: the way he stood with his hands in his pockets, the grain of the soil beneath his shoes, the exact angle of the evening light. But if she tried to hold one of those images for more than a second, her mind slammed a door on it before the picture could fully form. Because the memory came back so vividly and without warning, she began to see threads of it everywhere—in the grit under her fingernails after a repair, in the sound of footsteps behind her on the sidewalk, in any man who stood still too long.

The smell of soil was the worst trigger. Even now, when she walked from her garage to the parts supplier and passed a freshly turned garden bed, the scent would hit her nostrils and the photographic memory would snap open—the man, the dirt, the waiting—and she would feel her chest tighten. Stress did the same thing: a rush of work orders, a tight deadline, and the intrusive images would surface without warning. And what frightened her most was that feeling happy could also bring it back. A moment of relaxation, a laugh with a customer, and then suddenly the memory would intrude, as if her own contentment was a trap. She had come to believe that any moment of peace was dangerous, that pleasure itself signaled threat, and so she stayed taut, scanning, ready.

Linh had become hypervigilant in ways that exhausted her. She checked behind her constantly, even on the short walk from her house to the garage, her head swiveling to confirm no one was following. She was superalert and on guard, and the vigilance itself triggered more memories—a glance over her shoulder would summon the photographic image of the man behind her, and then she would be back in the fear. That fear made her hypersensitive to triggers: the more alert she was, the more she noticed the smell of soil on her own hands after wiping a greasy part, or the way stress buzzed in her ears, or the fleeting warmth of an unexpected happy moment. Each trigger looped back into a memory, and each memory kept her on guard.

At home, a place that should have been safe, Linh felt just as watchful. She checked the locks three times before bed, and she had stopped sitting in the armchair that faced the backyard because the scent of the neighbor's compost pile drifted in through the window. Her husband, a retired postal carrier, had learned not to surprise her from behind; she would flinch and snap, then feel ashamed. The avoidance had shaped her days: she worked longer hours at the garage to avoid the quiet evening hours, and she had stopped accepting help from unfamiliar customers, turning away work to keep strangers out of her bay. The isolation was wearing on her marriage, and her husband had gently suggested she talk to someone.

What finally brought Linh to the clinic was a morning when she walked into her garage and caught the faint smell of soil from a potted plant a customer had left on the counter. The photographic memory seized her—the man, the dirt, the waiting—and she could not move for several minutes. She had to sit down. She realized, staring at her trembling hands, that she was living inside a loop she could not break on her own. She was afraid of what the memories would do to her if she stayed this vigilant forever. But she was also terrified that letting the guard down would invite him back, even though she knew, logically, that he was gone. She came seeking help, she said, because she wanted to sleep through the night without the photographs, and because she wanted to feel the rain without the fear.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Memory → Triggers: No paragraph conveys that the trauma memory directly influences or increases triggers; the causal link is mediated by threat/hypervigilance.
  e.g. "After the memory had surfaced, even the most ordinary things — a kettle whistling, a door slamming — felt like warnings she couldn't afford to ignore."
  e.g. "The intrusive image left her scanning every room she entered, cataloguing exits, tracking faces, unable to switch off."
  e.g. "Because the memory came back so vividly, she began to see threads of it everywhere: in strangers' faces, in certain times of day, in the quality of winter light."
